items: About 23k pages per second; size the fleet by network bandwidth, not CPU.
Split fetching and parsing into separate stages with queues and stored raw pages, so each scales and retries on its own.
Respect per-domain rate limits and robots.txt, and skip already-seen URLs and duplicate content.
Crawl from seed URLs, fetch pages, extract text, follow links
Store text for LLM training: 10B pages in 5 days
Politeness: robots.txt, per-domain rate limits
Fault tolerant: resume without losing progress
No duplicate URLs or content
Efficient (network-bound)
10B ÷ 5 days ≈ 23k pages/s. × ~2MB ≈ 46GB/s, so size the fleet by network bandwidth, not CPU.
Raw storage ~20PB → S3.

blocks.text: Start with a frontier queue of URLs and fetcher workers pulling from it.
Split fetch (network-bound) from parse (CPU-bound) with S3 + a second queue. Each scales independently, and parsing can be re-run from stored HTML.

items: Split fetch (network-bound) from parse (CPU-bound) with S3 + a second queue. Each scales independently, and parsing can be re-run from stored HTML.
Politeness: per-domain token buckets and cached robots.txt in Redis. Not allowed yet? Re-queue with a delay (visibility timeout).
Extracted links pass a dedupe check (URL hash in DB or Bloom filter) before entering the frontier. Content hashes catch mirrored pages.
Why separate stages?
Different bottlenecks, independent scaling and retries, and you can re-parse 20PB without re-crawling.
Crash mid-crawl?
A message is acked only after the raw page is in S3: at-least-once, idempotent by URL hash.
Crawler traps?
Max depth per domain, URL normalization, content-hash dedupe.
DNS bottleneck?
Cache DNS per worker; multiple resolvers.
One monolithic fetch→parse loop: a slow parser stalls fetching and a crash loses in-flight work.
Adding parts before a number shows they are needed.
Ignoring retries, timeouts and crashes.
